title: Avesta — Yasna
dateDisplay: Gathas c. 1200–1000 BCE; liturgical prose c. 6th–4th century BCE
attributionNote: The Yasna is a liturgical compilation. Its seventeen Gathas are traditionally ascribed to Zarathushtra himself; the surrounding chapters are anonymous priestly compositions, and the Visparad, Âfrînagân and Gâh prayers belong to the same ritual corpus.
description: The Yasna is the chief liturgy of Zoroastrianism, in seventy-two chapters: the consecration of the sacred drink, the recital of the Ahuna Vairya and other prayers, confession of faith, invocations of the Bountiful Immortals, and at its centre the Gathas, the seventeen hymns ascribed to Zarathushtra. This volume adds the Visparad, the Âfrînagân blessings and the Gâh prayers that are recited with it.
historicalContext: The Yasna preserves the oldest Zoroastrian material in the Gathas, composed in archaic Avestan and transmitted orally for centuries before being written down. L. H. Mills translated the volume for the Sacred Books of the East (volume 31, 1887); his rendering is literal to the point of obscurity, but it remains a standard public-domain witness to the text.
availabilityNote: Complete for this volume. The Yasna (including the Gathas), Visparad, Âfrînagân and Gâh prayers are streamed from the Internet Sacred Text Archive at read time, one chapter per page. The volume's introduction and the fragments printed after the Gâhs are not part of the work.
